solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Total construction reduced to powder

indicators.note: the two words are cut down at both ends, leaving only the letters that straddle the gap

blocks.note: the tail of toTAL
the head of Construction

explanation.surface: A whole building collapses into dust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total' looks like the adjective for a wrecked building; it is just the first of two words whose join spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Talc is a soft mineral ground into a fine powder.

clue.text: In translation, reorder sad English poem

indicators.note: translating turns words into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone translating a gloomy English poem decides to rearrange it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorder' looks like the instruction but is fodder; 'In translation' does the rearranging. The poem is Robert Burns's 'A Red, Red Rose', which is Scots rather than English.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's 'A Red, Red Rose' is one of the best-known poems in the language.

clue.text: In post after tea covering for old soldiers

indicators.note: IN placed after CHA, and then the post follows

blocks.note: cha is an informal British word for tea
taken as written
post and mail are the same thing

explanation.surface: Tea is served to veterans once the letters have arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a teatime scene, but 'In' is simply the letters IN, sitting between the tea and the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain mail was the linked-metal armour worn by medieval soldiers.

clue.text: Seductive invitation to advance success with woman

indicators.note: puts HER alongside the earlier pieces

blocks.note: 'Come!' invites someone to approach
a hit is a success
HER stands for a woman

explanation.surface: A woman's alluring beckon wins her admirer over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invitation to advance' is not a pay rise or an army order; it is the single word COME.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom made adjective: a look that seems to say 'come here' is flirtatious, luring the viewer closer.

clue.text: Plant early bird among spies

indicators.note: the bird goes among the spies, inside CIA

blocks.note: the American intelligence agency
the lark sings at dawn, and an early riser is a lark; it sits inside CIA

explanation.surface: An agent who rises at dawn is planted in an espionage ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a verb for placing a mole; it is the noun, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarkia is a genus of flowering garden plants.

clue.text: Consume such fine ham, prepared all alike

indicators.note: food is prepared by being worked into a new state, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation to eat some good ham, all cooked the same way.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is using all of 'fine' as fodder, which leaves a spare I; only its abbreviation F goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are much of a muchness are very nearly the same.

clue.text: Fish finger girl needs for this?

blocks.note: HER stands for a girl
what the girl needs for her finger is a ring

explanation.surface: Something a girl needs if she wants to eat fish fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish finger' pretends to be the breaded snack; split it after 'Fish'. 'finger ... needs for this?' is a cryptic hint at what goes on a finger, with 'needs' tying the girl to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The herring is a common North Atlantic food fish.

clue.text: Flier put name to protagonist

indicators.note: to put one thing to another is to set it against it, so N is placed beside HERO
N is added to the end of HERO

blocks.note: the protagonist of a story is its hero
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A pilot signs their name to the lead role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests an aviator; it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A heron is a large wading bird, so something that flies.

clue.text: Band touring almost every region

indicators.note: the band goes round, so REM encircles the rest
ALL loses its final letter

blocks.note: R.E.M., the American rock band
ALL (every) cut short, sitting inside REM

explanation.surface: A band on tour visits nearly every part of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' seems to be the band's travels; a tour goes round a circuit, which is the container signal. R.E.M. is an American rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a kingdom or sphere is a realm, and both are regions under one rule.

clue.text: I don’t believe you coach robbers in this?

blocks.note: 'Get away!' is an exclamation of disbelief
a railway coach is a car

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of training robbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' reads as a verb, to train; it is the noun, a carriage. The question mark flags that 'robbers in this' only hints at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Robbers flee a crime scene in a getaway car.

clue.text: Small boat for start of adventure

indicators.note: take only the first letter of 'adventure'

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
first letter of adventure

explanation.surface: A little boat is ready for the beginning of a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' looks like a link word; it is PRO. A proa is a Malay outrigger boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A proa is a small sailing boat with an outrigger, from Malaysia.

clue.text: Barman in clubs given free clothing

indicators.note: FRANK clothes C, wrapping it inside

blocks.note: frank means candid, open, free in speech
C is the card-suit abbreviation, placed inside FRANK

explanation.surface: A bartender at a nightclub is handed some clothes for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' is not a bartender but a man of musical bars: César Franck, the composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer writes music in bars, so César Franck is a bar man.

clue.text: Herb returning a cheque, only half of amount

indicators.note: going back, so A GIRO is read backwards
keep just the first half of NUMBER

blocks.note: a giro is a British cheque, for example one paying benefits; read backwards it is ORIGA
an amount is a number; only its first half, NUM, is kept

explanation.surface: Someone returns a cheque for a herb, having paid only half.
explanation.walkthrough: Halving 'amount' itself gives nothing useful; it is its synonym NUMBER that is halved.
explanation.definitionFit: Origanum is the plant genus of marjoram and oregano.

clue.text: Busy with score of satisfactory quality

indicators.note: puts SCRATCH alongside UP TO

blocks.note: being up to something is being busy with it
to score a surface is to scratch it

explanation.surface: A composer is busy with a score of acceptable standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' is not music or points but a mark scored into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that is up to scratch meets the required standard.

clue.text: Fish beginning to acquire thought

indicators.note: take only the first letter of 'acquire'

blocks.note: the ide is a freshwater fish
first letter of acquire

explanation.surface: Someone starts thinking about buying a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The ide, a European freshwater fish, is a crossword regular worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a notion that comes to mind is both an idea and a thought.

clue.text: A minute seaweed and partner combine

indicators.note: 'and' means plus, so MATE is joined on after the other pieces

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for minute
seaweed is an alga
a mate is a partner

explanation.surface: A tiny scrap of seaweed teams up with a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minute' reads as tiny, describing the seaweed; it is the time unit, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: companies that merge into a single body amalgamate, or combine.

clue.text: Referred to people I noted wandering about

indicators.note: letters that wander about end up in a new order

blocks.note: men are people
I NOTED rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recalls spotting a few people roaming around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Referred to' could be any verb phrase; the past tense points to -ED, which this anagram supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: To mention something is to refer to it.

clue.text: Do like senior executive: toss one diamond after another on table?

definitions.text: toss one diamond after another on table?

blocks.note: a 'suit' is slang for an executive, and doing like one means copying the lead

blocks.clueFragment: toss one diamond after another on table?
blocks.note: in card games, playing a card of the suit led, such as diamond on diamond

explanation.surface: A junior copies the boss, even down to tossing diamonds on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'suit' is slang for an executive, so copying one is following a suit. The question mark marks the card-table sense as playful.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow suit is to do what others have just done, as in cards.

clue.text: Signal extremely short period of time checks

indicators.note: take only the extreme letters of 'short'
to check something is to hold it in, so WHILE holds ST

blocks.note: a while is a period of time
first and last letters of short, held inside WHILE

explanation.surface: A brief spell of timing is interrupted by a warning sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'checks' is a verb here: it restrains, holding the letters in.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a referee blows a sharp whistle to signal a stop, and to whistle is to signal.

clue.text: Drank regularly, with Oscar for one, and fell over

indicators.note: O takes the place of one, I

blocks.note: to tipple is to drink habitually
Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet
I is the Roman numeral one; O replaces it

explanation.surface: Someone who kept drinking, Oscar among them, fell down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letters instruction; it belongs to the definition of TIPPLED. 'for one' is not 'for example' but O in place of I.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tower that loses balance and crashes down has toppled.

clue.text: Scoff about withdrawing appeal for silence

indicators.note: drawing back, so ON is read backwards

blocks.note: on means about, concerning; turned back it is NO
'Sh!' asks for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a withdrawn request for quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' reads as mock; it is the other sense, to eat greedily. Nosh is British slang for food or eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Both scoff and nosh are British slang for eating greedily.

clue.text: Big stone landed hard on a valuable one lying around

indicators.note: in an across clue, LIT and H come after MEGA
turned round, so A GEM reads MEGA

blocks.note: a gem is a valuable stone; turned round, A GEM gives MEGA
a bird that lit on a branch landed on it
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A huge rock came down heavily on a precious stone left lying about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a valuable one' refers back to 'stone': a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: A megalith is a large standing stone, such as those at Stonehenge.

clue.text: Naughty girl, they say, wearing these?

definitions.note: the definition is 'these', the furs a minx might wear

indicators.note: signals that the answer is said like MINX

blocks.note: a minx is a cheeky or flirtatious girl

explanation.surface: A saucy girl dressed in these furs.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only 'these'; the question mark admits that it is defined by what the minx wears.
explanation.definitionFit: Mink coats, or minks, are the furs a glamorous flirt might wear.

clue.text: Odd that doctor’s admitting man with bellyache

indicators.note: the doctor lets RUM in, so GP surrounds it

blocks.note: a GP is a family doctor in Britain (general practitioner)
rum is British slang for odd; it sits inside GP

explanation.surface: It is strange that the doctor is taking in a man with stomach pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bellyache' reads as a stomach ailment for the doctor; it is the verb sense, to complain.
explanation.definitionFit: A grump is a grumbler, one who bellyaches.

clue.text: Religious house overlooking crucial thing in urgent matter

indicators.note: to overlook something is to leave it out, so IT is dropped

blocks.note: an urgent matter is a priority
IT is the thing that matters ('this is it'); drop it from PRIORITY

explanation.surface: A monastery ignores the key point of a pressing business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' suggests a building with a view; it means omitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A priory is a religious house run by a prior or prioress.

clue.text: Common sense surely not useless

blocks.note: 'No!' is a cry of disbelief
U/S stands for unserviceable, so useless

explanation.surface: Common sense is surely no waste of time.
explanation.walkthrough: US for useless is the British abbreviation U/S, unserviceable. Nous is British English for practical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal use, from the Greek for mind: someone with the wit to handle everyday matters has nous.

clue.text: Noted suite set out following specific blueprint

indicators.note: letters set out are laid out afresh, so rearranged
what follows comes behind, so the rearranged SET is placed after THE PLAN

blocks.note: the definite article singles out something specific
a blueprint is a plan
SET rearranged, coming last

explanation.surface: A hotel suite is arranged according to a precise plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' means musical, in notes, so the 'suite' is not rooms but Holst's orchestral suite.
explanation.definitionFit: Holst's The Planets is a celebrated orchestral suite.

clue.text: Taken to court to keep quiet urge prohibited

indicators.note: SUED keeps the rest inside it

blocks.note: to take someone to court is to sue them
P, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
to urge is to press; P and PRESS go inside SUED

explanation.surface: Someone was sued to silence an urge that had been banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prohibited' is the definition in its past-participle sense, banned.
explanation.definitionFit: Something suppressed has been banned or kept from view.

clue.text: Children’s author was made to turn left

indicators.note: HAD is turned round to give DAH

blocks.note: 'had to' means was made to; HAD turned round gives DAH
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A children's writer was forced to change direction and go left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was made to' reads as one phrase; split it, since 'was made' is HAD and 'to turn' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and many other children's books.
